newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Russia's U.N. ambassador says NY police biased.
newsitem.headline: Russia's U.N. ambassador says NY police biased.

text.p: Russia's U.N. ambassador Sergei Lavrov on Thursday firmly rejected charges from the New York proseuctor's office about one of his diplomats, saying the man and his colleague from Belarus were beaten by police.

He said that a determination from the Manhattan District Attorney's office on Wednesday that the two should be prosecuted was "one-sided" and that he had not received any word from the State Department, which deals with foreign diplomats in such cases.

The incident on December 29 involved Boris Obnossov of Russia's U.N, mission and Yuri Orange of the Belarus mission, both first secretaries. Police said they pulled Obnossov from a car because he appeared intoxicated after parking illegally near a fire hydrant. Orange then was said to have punched one of the officers.

District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said the police acted reasonably and that the evidence would support criminal charges, including driving while intoxicated, resisting arrest, harassment and disorderly conduct.
According to Lavrov, Russia had received a fax from Morgenthau and "he clearly took one side and ruled the diplomats were driving while drunk"

He said the incident happened after they left a restaruant and not while driving and that police prevented them from using the car afterwards. Since the police never offered or gave the driver a test to determine if he was drinking "he cannot be accused of being drunk.
The district attorney, he said, "ignored all the evidence the Russian side provided and of a witness, an American witness, who saw what happened and contradicted the police report."
It was an "unjustifiable attack on Russian and Belarussian diplomats," he added.

Lavrov, who is this month's Security Council president known for his articulate and sometimes acerbic comments, said he had not heard from State Department officials and expected any official communications from them.

He said he took comfort that Morgenthau had recognised in his statement the diplomatic immunity provided for diplomats. "This immunity was taken from them when police decided to beat them on December 29," he said.

Mayor Rudolph Giuliani followed up the incident by wanting to remove special license plates of diplomats who routinely ignored parking tickets, kicking off a row between the envoys and New York police and city officials.
Bill Richardson, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, first agreed but then said the Giuliani plan plan should be modified. The issue still has not been settled.

In the meantime Richardson said hostility towards foreign diplomats was increasing in New York and New York police appeared to be harrassing diplomats by deliberately targeting some of them in issuing parking fines.
